extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; polite, literate public and moralists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and normative criteria about the use and limits of pleasantry (wit/humour) in social/company settings, plus related moral and stylistic rules (modesty, vanity, and a poetic translation technique). Emphases include when pleasantry is beneficial or corrosive, and a technique for preserving surprise in sacred/poetic translation.

rubrics_metrics.name: True modesty vs false modesty
rubrics_metrics.description: True Modesty is ashamed to do any thing that is repugnant to the Rules of right Reason: False Modesty is ashamed to do any thing that is opposite to the Humour of the Company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True modesty guards virtue and is limited by prudence and religion; false modesty is an undetermined instinct that leads people to do ill or indiscreet things to avoid appearing singular or unfashionable. Examples/anti-patterns: lending money you cannot spare, recommending strangers, accepting obligations you disapprove of, or complying with vices because 'that's the fashion'—these are symptoms of vicious (false) modesty. Xenophanes' remark (I dare not do any ill thing) is offered as an exemplar of virtuous timorousness versus cowardly compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity over hypocrisy in religious conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypocrisie cannot indeed be too much detested, but at the same time is to be preferred to open Impiety; the due Mean is to be sincerely Virtuous, and at the same time to let the World see we are so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid perverted modesty that hides devotion; while hypocrisy is worse for the possessor, openness about true virtue is the correct mean. The writer warns against taking pains to conceal piety out of fear of ridicule (which leads to the disappearance of ordinary Christian deportment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Morality should have pre-eminence and faith must support it
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion divides into Faith (what we are to believe) and Morality (what we are to practise); Morality has the pre-eminence in several respects and a perfect person is defective in neither.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons given: morality is more fixed/eternal; morality alone can make a person beneficial to mankind; morality quiets the mind and advances private happiness; moral rules are more certain across nations; virtuous infidels may have hope where vicious believers do not; faith draws much of its excellency from its influence on morality. Practical maxims: avoid making any article of faith that does not confirm or improve morality; reject any article of faith that weakens practical religion; in dubious matters consider ill consequences before assent (e.g., persecution for conscience' sake).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh consequences before acting on disputable doctrines
rubrics_metrics.description: In all dubious Points, consider any ill Consequences that may arise from them, supposing they should be Erroneous, before we give up our Assent to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied example: prosecuting men for conscience' sake produces hatred, ensnaring false professions, social exclusion, bodily affliction, ruined fortunes and families, or death. Therefore one should require a very high degree of certainty (as in a mathematical demonstration) before acting on such principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation technique: conceal the divine subject for surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: On translating Psalm CXIV: 'the Poet utterly conceals the Presence of God in the Beginning of it... For if God had appeared before, there could be no wonder why the Mountains should leap...' — therefore the name is not mentioned till afterward to preserve surprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rule for sacred/poetic translation: preserve the structural device of withholding the subject (or reveal) to create effect; use possessive constructions where appropriate instead of naming the divine subject immediately. Aim to 'preserve what I could of the Spirit of the sacred Author' and to avoid mere paraphrase; imitate the original devices that produce surprise and majesty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasantry's social force and its double edge
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasantry in Company has great force: a man's faults are generally overlooked if he is pleasant; a certain carelessness that attends pleasantry carries him forward more successfully than diligence and assiduity do others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive case: when pleasantry accompanies manly and virtuous sentiments it gives great pleasure. Negative case: when pleasantry stands alone it gilds many ill qualities—breaking promises, ill-nature in domestic life, selfishness—and makes the 'pleasant fellow' socially tolerated despite moral failures (examples: Dacinthus; stories of King Charles II). Evaluation criterion: judge pleasantry both by its social effect (does it excuse or conceal harm?) and by the character it accompanies (virtue vs vice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour must not be a shield for vice or cruelty
rubrics_metrics.description: A very pleasant Fellow shall turn your good Name to a Jest, make your Character contemptible, debauch your Wife or Daughter, and yet be received by the rest of the World with Welcome where-ever he appears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not allow wit/pleasantry to be used as an excuse for injuring others or committing immoral acts. When evaluating a comic persona or social wit, penalize uses of humour that inflict pain, degrade reputation, or serve only self-satisfaction; laud uses that accompany benevolence and virtuous sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid social salutations and diversion during solemn worship
rubrics_metrics.description: Ceremonies, bows, courtseys, whisperings, smiles, winks, nods, and other familiar arts of salutation that take up so much time in churches are inconsistent with the duty and true intent of entering into religious assemblies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Behavioural criterion for conduct in religious settings: maintain solemn engagement rather than social display. The essay recommends the more reserved demeanour observed in Roman Catholic churches and among Mahometans as laudable patterns for the purpose of public worship. Anti-pattern: treating service as an occasion to catalogue others' dress or to perform elaborate salutations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs and consequences of vanity and following popular opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Vanity, Self-Conceit, Flattery, Affectation, and Fashion seduce people into a false estimation of themselves; Popular Opinion and Errour bewitch people into the 'Paradise of Fools'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation of character/works: identify flattery, affectation, and fashion as devices that falsely embellish merit. The allegory: Vanity's palace is built on illusion (curling clouds, rainbow-painted paths); following it leads to Scorn, Poverty, Infamy, and other harms when the delusion ends. Recommend plain-dealing and resistance to flattering public opinion as marks of sound judgement.
